title: The problem of waste in the 21st century

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: In 1962, engineer Sten Gustaf Thulin invented a packaging material which could be divided into individual shopping bags at checkouts. Today, in New Zealand, we use a billion of these single-use plastic shopping bags annually. It's only a few local councils that accept them in recycling collections, and just a handful of supermarkets that offer the same service, In North America, it's an approximate 100 billion bags a year, a far higher number, but unsurprising, given the greater population. But where do they end up? A 2014 study estimated that over five trillion pieces of plastic are now floating in the ocean. Shopping bags account for much of that waste. Even when plastic bags are sent to council landfills, the massive sites where rubbish is dumped, this still creates problems. The length of time it takes for bags to break down and biodegrade depends on how much sunlight they're exposed to. If exposed the whole time, it might take ten years. At the bottom of landfills, it might take a century. Researchers also suspect that plastic bags don't actually break down completely, but just become microscopic pieces which then find their way into rivers and streams, and into soil. This may have a worse ecological impact than we yet understand.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: What can be done about this situation? Last January, Waveney Warth and her husband Matthew decided to send nothing to the landfill for twelve months. To achieve this, they rejected any packaging made of plastic or non-recyclable material. Instead, they bought food and other products locally, Meat came from their butcher in paper. They baked their own bread. In her blog Warth maintains the power to change things and force manufacturers to use recyclable materials lies with customers, but admits that multi-million dollars marketing campaigns are hard to fight.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Not everyone is willing, of course, to maintain such a zero-waste lifestyle, and rely instead on their council-provided recycling bins for their plastic and glass bottles. Yuri Schokking is an area manager for Smart Environmental, a company that runs a recycling facility for these materials. He feels that the contents of an individual bin can reveal a lot about human nature: plastic cream bottles still half-full, plastic trays still containing meat, for example, the things people could not be bothered to clean or dispose of properly. The council now sends out letters to residents, warning them their bins will no longer be emptied if they continue to use them for general rubbish. Collection trucks have recently been fitted with high-tech cameras, so they can easily record the contents of each bin and can match the bin to an address.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Thousands of plastic bottles are stored in Schokking's warehouse at any one time, then crushed by a 70-tonne machine, called a 'press', into a plastic block. The blocks can be loaded into a shipping container. They are then sent 'to China and other Asian destinations that already have their own huge volumes of waste,' Schokking says, explaining that this is where 'investment in re- processing facilities is worthwhile and sustainable.' He says that re-processing recyclable plastic and turning it into new products is impossible to do in New Zealand because of its small population. In other words, New Zealanders would need to consume more plastic to make a re-processing operation cost-effective and possible over the long term.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Other kinds of rubbish are problematic, too. David Stephenson is responsible for recycling and rubbish collection at the council. Until last year, New Zealand had yearly inorganic collections, meaning people could put rubbish such as broken furniture and appliances outside their house to be collected at no charge. Since councils across New Zealand have made the decision to withdraw this service, and make people pay to dispose of unwanted items, the unfortunate result of this decision can already be seen. David knows some people are unwilling to meet the full costs of disposal. 'People say, "Well, I don't like that price, so I'm going to find an alternative".' He says that alternative is often driving down a remote rural road and throwing rubbish from the car onto farm land. Auckland Council spends $900,000 annually cleaning it up.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: But it's not just rubbish and recyclable goods people throw away. Volunteers at Kaibosh Food Rescue collect surplus food from retailers, mostly that's good enough to eat but not sell, and redistribute it to people in need. Kaibosh's Matt Dagger says, 'Nearly 40 per cent of food waste happens before it gets to markets: carrots are misshapen, or fruit the wrong colour. I'm disgusted by the degree of waste that industry and consumers seem to tolerate when there are so many people without the financial means to feed their family.'

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: In some ways, reducing food waste may be easier than making efforts to recycle its packaging. But is recycling the way forward? No, says Alison Singer of environmental organisation Worldwatch, which claims that, by easing people's conscience, recycling encourages high consumption habits. Research proves its point: recycling rates are rising, but household expenditure also jumped by 57% over the last twenty years: we are buying more clothing, household goods and takeaways. The idea that if we each do a little bit, we car. save our world, creates a fantasy that our individual responsibility to the environment is minimal. Singer feels the government emphasis on recycling places undue responsibility for waste on consumers, when it's producers who continue to deliver over-packaged goods without penalty.
